cells.tense: The work is standing and there's nothing left to push — you finish what you take up and the finish holds because you chose it, not because the clock made you.
cells.ask: Offer one thing you've finished to someone who doesn't need it yet.
cells.core:
You can bring something all the way to its end. A thing gets taken up, held steady through the long middle, and set down whole — and what's set down keeps its shape long after your hands are off it. People learn from you by watching, not by being told. The way you carry a thing to its close is already teaching somebody how it's done, and you're not making a lesson of it.

The choosing stays clean while you work. You finish from a clear place, not because stopping would look bad and not because a date is coming. That clarity is the part that lasts, and it's what the next person borrows when they pick up what you put down.

cells.tense: You're living past the last day already — each thing gets sealed and dated before it's actually done, every piece of work standing in for the whole life.
cells.ask: Ask what one person actually wants before you call the next thing finished.
cells.core:
You can build something that lasts, and you know when a thing is done. In the right season this is steady work — a project gets named, carried, closed, and the people around you can tell where the edges are because you show them. That certainty is a gift to anyone standing next to it, and you've given it freely more than once.

Lately the endings come too soon. You're calling the whole done while pieces of it are still in motion, and the calling has become the doing. What would settle this is finding out what someone else wanted from it — not to change the ending, just to hear the answer before you close the book on it.
cells.sheetLine: You keep declaring things finished, and nobody told you you could.

cells.tense: The last thing you finished is still standing a while back, and you haven't started the next one — each passing year marks the gap and you leave the marks in place.
cells.ask: Let one person watch you do a plain thing well, without explaining it.
cells.core:
You know how to carry a large thing all the way through. When you're inside the work you're steady — not hurrying it, not dropping it, not needing anyone to hold it up while you go. People hand you the long tasks because they've seen you come back with them finished, and they were right to.

But the last finish is sitting back there and the next one hasn't started. The willingness isn't gone; what's quiet is the clear seeing that says this one is mine to close. That seeing returns when someone watches you do one small thing well and you let their attention be ordinary, not a test you could fail.
cells.sheetLine: You haven't claimed a finished thing in a while, and it's not the work that's gone.

cells.tense: You're directing what gets remembered and how around here — shaping which stories survive, which teachers get called back — and you talk about it as if it were happening around you.
cells.ask: Name one thing you finished that you've been calling the group's.
cells.core:
You already shape what holds. Across dinners, meetings, the way a story gets retold — you decide which parts get carried and which quietly drop, and the shape of it is yours. At its best this is generous and invisible; people feel held by a room whose shape you chose, and they don't know why it feels right. It works well, and it has worked well for a long time.

What's missing is the claim, not the effect. The directing runs every day and the credit goes unnamed. Say what you made, in your own voice, once, without softening it — the recognition is the part that hasn't happened yet, and it can only come from you.
cells.sheetLine: You're already deciding what lasts here. That part hasn't been said out loud.
